newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bodo tribal militants gun down rivals.
newsitem.headline: India's Bodo tribal militants gun down rivals.

text.p: Bodo tribal guerrillas shot dead nine members of a rival group early on Monday in the northeastern Indian state of Assam, police said.
The victims, from the same tribe, were gunned down at Barama, 75 km (46 miles) west of Guwahati, Assam's biggest city, they said.
"The guerrillas of Bodoland Army are suspected to be involved in the attack," a senior police officer told Reuters in Guwahati.

The Bodoland Army is an extremist group which wants a separate nation for about 800,000 Bodo tribals who live north of the mighty Brahmaputra river in the state, which has a population of 25 million people.
Activists of the main Bodo movement are fighting for a separate province they want carved out of Assam.
In 1993, moderate Bodo leaders settled for an autonomous council after a series of negotiations with the government.
But a section of Bodo youth, dissatisfied with the council, raised the demand for a separate Bodo country and formed the Bodoland Army.
Bodo militants stepped up their campaign after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda came to Guwahati in October last year offering development funds but no hope of independence or autonomy.

On December 30, guerrillas of the Bodoland Liberation Tigers Force (BLTF), which wants a separate province, bombed a railway track about 200 km (125 miles) west of Guwahati. The blast ripped through a crowded express train and killed at least 34 passengers.
Since 1987, Bodos have been fighting immigrants, security forces and, at times, themselves. Police say some 5,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence.
